opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me, it's great to be here.

Honestly, it's been remarkable, and a bit surreal. When I started working on generative models, it was a fairly niche area. Most of the excitement in machine learning was around discriminative tasks like classification, where you have labeled data and a clear objective. Generative modeling seemed much harder, almost a curiosity. The samples we could produce were blurry, low resolution, and you could immediately tell they were fake. There was a lot of debate about whether it was even a worthwhile direction, beyond being an interesting theoretical problem.

What kept me interested was the belief that learning to generate data forces a model to understand the structure of the world in a deep way. If you can generate realistic images or coherent text, you must have captured something meaningful about the underlying distribution. That idea has turned out to be even more powerful than many of us expected.

There have been several key turning points. GANs showed that you could get sharp, realistic samples, although they were notoriously hard to train. Then autoregressive models and transformers really took off for language. In my group we spent a lot of time on score-based models, which became closely connected to diffusion models. The insight there was that instead of modeling the probability density directly, you can learn the gradient of the log density, the score, at different noise levels, and then use that to gradually turn noise into data. That gave us stable training, excellent sample quality, and a principled mathematical framework, and it ended up powering a lot of the image, video, and audio generation systems people use today.

What surprises me most is how quickly things moved from research to products used by millions of people. A few years ago generating a photorealistic image from a text prompt felt like science fiction, and now it's almost taken for granted. At the same time, I think we're still early. There are many open questions about efficiency, controllability, reliability, and how to bring these ideas to new domains like science, molecules, and materials. So I'm very excited, both by how far we've come and by how much is still left to figure out.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts early blurry, low-resolution samples with modern photorealistic generation, but it does not mention MNIST or the circa-2014 capability level.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, it's been pretty remarkable to watch. When I started working on generative models, the whole field felt very niche. We were training models on things like MNIST digits, and if you could generate a reasonably convincing handwritten "3," that was considered a result. The question people would ask was almost philosophical: why would you even want to model the distribution of your data? The practical applications were not obvious at all.

What changed, I think, is a combination of a few things coming together. One was the algorithmic side. Early on, we had a few families of approaches, like variational autoencoders, GANs, autoregressive models, and each had real limitations. GANs could produce sharp samples but were unstable and hard to train. Likelihood-based models were principled but produced blurry or lower-quality outputs. A lot of my own work, and the work of my students, was around trying to find a framework that gave you both: a stable training objective and high sample quality. Score-based and diffusion models ended up being one answer to that, and it's been gratifying to see that line of thinking scale the way it has.

The second thing was scale, plain and simple. The ideas that worked on tiny benchmarks turned out to keep working as you threw more compute and data at them, which wasn't guaranteed. And once that became clear, the amount of effort and investment flowing into the area exploded.

So if you ask me how I view the progress, I'd say it has exceeded what I would have predicted on almost every axis. Images, video, audio, protein structures, and of course language. The surprising part is less that any one of these became possible and more that so many of them fell to essentially the same small set of ideas.

That said, I try to stay a little grounded about it. There are still fundamental questions we don't have good answers to. Why do these models generalize the way they do? How do we make them efficient, because right now generating a sample from a diffusion model is expensive? How do we get them to reason reliably rather than just produce plausible-looking output? A lot of the excitement is deserved, but I think the research questions underneath are still very much open, and that's the part that keeps it interesting for me.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts early MNIST results with much broader capabilities today, but it does not place the early state of the field around 2014.

astra-6.text:
It’s been remarkable. When I started working in this area, a lot of the challenge was simply getting models to capture relatively simple distributions. Images were small, the results were often blurry, and even evaluating whether a model had learned something useful was difficult.

Now we have models that generate convincing images, write code, and sustain a conversation. The gap between what seemed possible in research and what people can actually use has narrowed dramatically. I think the scale of that progress has been surprising, even for people working in the field.

At the same time, generating something plausible is only part of the problem. Can we trust the output? Can we control it? Can we use these models to help solve scientific problems where there’s a right answer, rather than just an answer that looks good? Those are some of the questions that make this a very exciting time.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts earlier small, often blurry images with today’s stronger capabilities, but it does not communicate the specific starting point of barely modeling MNIST images around 2014.

sol-6.1.text:
When I started working in this area, we were already interested in the idea of learning a distribution from data and then generating new examples. But there was a big gap between that ambition and what we could actually do. You could demonstrate these ideas on small datasets, but the samples were often pretty easy to distinguish from real data.

What’s been remarkable is seeing those same underlying questions lead to systems that can produce convincing images, text, and other kinds of data. It’s been a combination of better modeling ideas, more computation, more data, and a lot of engineering. I don’t think you can attribute the progress to just one of those things.

The other big change is that generation has become a way of interacting with models and solving problems. You’re not just asking whether a model can generate a realistic image; you’re asking whether you can guide it toward something useful. That opens up a much broader set of applications, including scientific ones. There are still fundamental questions about reliability and understanding what these models have learned, but the range of things we can now explore is really exciting.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts weak early results on small datasets with today’s convincing outputs, but it does not mention MNIST or around 2014.
